units.title: Hello, Solidity
units.summary: Write your first smart contract, learn what deploying and calling mean, and return text from a function.

lesson.md: Solidity is a language for **smart contracts**. A smart contract is a program that runs on a **blockchain**: a shared database that thousands of computers keep in sync. Nobody can change a contract after it is on the blockchain, and anyone can use it.

Line by line: `pragma solidity ^0.8.20;` tells the compiler which versions of Solidity the code needs. `^0.8.20` means version 0.8.20 or any newer 0.8 version. `contract Hello` starts a contract called `Hello`, and its code goes between the braces `{` and `}`.

`function greet()` defines a function called `greet`. `public` means that anyone can call it. `pure` means that it does not read or change any stored data. `returns (string memory)` says that the function gives back a `string`, which is text. `memory` means the text is a temporary value. `return` sends the value back, and every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.

A contract does nothing until you **deploy** it. First the compiler turns your code into bytecode for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). Then you send the bytecode to the blockchain in a **transaction**, a signed request to the network. The contract gets its own **address**, a long number such as `0xd9145CCE52D386f254917e481eB44e9943F39138` that identifies it. After that, you and others can **call** its functions.

How to read the examples in this course: every contract that has an output is deployed fresh. Then the calls that the text names run in the given order. Each call that returns a value adds one line with that value to the output. Text values appear without quotes. For the next contract, the calls are `bye()`, `hello()` and `bye()` again.

Every transaction costs **gas**: a small fee for the work the computers of the network do. Deploying a contract is a transaction, so it costs gas. Calling a `pure` function from outside only reads, so it is free. Functions that change data cost gas, and more work costs more gas.

You can try every example in Remix, a free online editor for Solidity that runs in the browser. Real Solidity files usually start with a license line such as `// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT`. The examples leave it out to stay short, so the compiler shows a warning about it.
Solidity is case sensitive: `contract` works, `Contract` does not. Text goes in double quotes, and a missing `;` at the end of a statement stops the compiler.

card: `function f() public pure returns (string memory)` returns text
Deploy = send the contract in a transaction; then call its functions

units.title: Types and state variables
units.summary: Store numbers, true/false values, text and addresses in state variables and local variables.

lesson.md: Every variable in Solidity has a **type**, and you write the type before the name. A **state variable** is declared inside the contract but outside any function. Its value is stored on the blockchain and stays there between calls.

`uint256` holds a whole number that is never negative. `bool` holds `true` or `false`. `string` holds text. When a state variable is `public`, Solidity creates a **getter**: a function with the same name that returns the value. The calls here are `balance()`, `open()` and `owner()`.

`int256` holds whole numbers that can be negative. `uint` is a short name for `uint256`, and `int` for `int256`. Solidity has no decimal numbers. You calculate with `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%`. The division `/` drops the remainder, and `%` gives the remainder. The calls are `temperature()`, `divide()` and `remainder()`.

`a` and `b` above are **local variables**. They are declared inside a function, exist only while it runs and are never stored. A state variable keeps its value. A state variable without a value starts with a default: `0` for numbers, `false` for `bool` and `""` for `string`.

A function that changes a state variable is neither `pure` nor `view`, so you leave that word out. Calling it is a transaction that costs gas. It returns nothing, so it adds no line to the output. The calls here are `count()`, `increment()`, `increment()` and `count()`.

An `address` holds the address of an account or a contract: 20 bytes written in hex, such as `0x5B38Da6a701c568545dCfcB03FcB875f56beddC4`. `msg.sender` is the address that calls the function or deploys the contract. Its default value is the zero address. In this course you use the address above, the first test account in Remix. A second account, Bob, has the address `0xAb8483F64d9C6d1EcF9b849Ae677dD3315835cb2`. In call lists, `you` and `bob` stand for these two addresses.
A local `string` variable needs the word `memory`, for example `string memory name = "Ada";`. Numbers, `bool` and `address` do not need it.

card: `bool` is `true` or `false`, `string` is text, `address` is an account
State variables are stored; local variables live only during a call

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write functions with parameters and return values, choose their visibility, and use view and pure.

lesson.md: A function can take **parameters**: values that the caller passes in. You write each parameter as a type and a name, separated by commas. The calls here are `add(2, 3)` and `add(10, 20)`.
A `string` parameter needs `memory`, like a local `string`. `string.concat` joins several texts into one. The call here is `greet("Ada")`.

A `view` function reads state variables but does not change them. A `pure` function neither reads nor changes them. A function without either word may change state. The compiler checks this: a `pure` function that reads a state variable does not compile. The calls here are `total(3)`, `setPrice(25)` and `total(3)`.

The **visibility** says who can call a function. `public`: everyone, from outside and from inside the contract. `external`: only from outside. `internal`: only code inside this contract and contracts built on it. `private`: only code inside this contract. Below, `tax` is a private helper: `withTax` can use it, but you cannot call it from outside. The call is `withTax(50)`.

A function can return several values. You list their types in `returns (...)` and write `return (a, b);`. In the output, the values appear on one line, separated by a comma. The call here is `divide(17, 5)`.
A `view` function that changes a state variable does not compile. Only leave out `view` and `pure` when the function really changes data, because then every call is a transaction that costs gas.

card: `view` reads state, `pure` reads and changes nothing

units.title: Decisions and require
units.summary: Choose between code paths with if and else, and stop bad calls with require and revert.

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. `else` runs code when it is `false`. The condition goes in parentheses. You compare values with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. The calls here are `grade(95)`, `grade(70)` and `grade(20)`.

Solidity checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is `true`. `&&` means and: both sides must be `true`. `||` means or: at least one side must be `true`. `!` turns `true` into `false` and back. The calls are `canVote(20, true)`, `canVote(20, false)` and `canVote(15, true)`.

A contract must stop when a call makes no sense. `require(condition, "message")` checks the condition. When it is `false`, the call **reverts**: it stops, undoes every change it made and returns the message. The gas used so far is still paid. In the output, a reverted call shows `revert:` and the message. The calls are `withdraw(30)`, `withdraw(500)` and `amount()`.

A revert undoes changes even when they happen before the check. Below, the second call `add(8)` first sets `count` to 12, then `require` fails, so `count` goes back to 4. The calls are `add(4)`, `add(8)` and `count()`. `+=` adds to a variable: `count += n` is short for `count = count + n`. In the same way, `-=` subtracts.

`revert("message")` stops the call without a condition. You use it inside an `if`. `require(ok, "message")` does the same as `if (!ok) { revert("message"); }`. The calls are `price(10)`, `price(30)` and `price(2)`.
Check the inputs at the start of a function, before you change anything. Keep messages short: every byte of a message makes the contract bigger.
Do not mix up `=` and `==`. `=` stores a value, `==` compares two values. A condition must be a `bool`, so `if (x = 5)` does not compile.

card: A revert undoes every change of the call

units.title: Loops and arrays
units.summary: Repeat code with for and while, and keep lists of values in fixed and dynamic arrays.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats code. In the parentheses you write three parts, separated by `;`: the start (`uint256 i = 1`), the condition to keep going (`i <= n`) and the step after each round (`i++`). `i++` adds 1 to `i`, and `i--` subtracts 1. The calls here are `sumTo(4)` and `sumTo(10)`.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. Here it halves `n` until it reaches 1 and counts the steps. The calls are `steps(8)` and `steps(20)`.

An **array** is a list of values of one type. `uint256[]` is a **dynamic** array: it can grow. `push(x)` adds `x` at the end, `pop()` removes the last item, and `length` gives the number of items. Items are numbered from 0, so `scores[1]` is the second item. A public array gets a getter that takes the index. The calls are `add(70)`, `add(30)`, `add(90)`, `count()` and `scores(1)`.

A function can return a whole array with `returns (uint256[] memory)`. The output shows an array in square brackets. A loop from `0` while `i < scores.length` visits every item once. The calls are `add(70)`, `add(30)`, `add(90)`, `all()` and `total()`.

A **fixed** array has a size that never changes, for example `uint256[3]`. It has no `push`. Inside a function, `new uint256[](n)` creates a temporary array with `n` items that all start at 0. The calls are `temps(2)` and `squares(4)`.

Every round of a loop costs gas. A loop over an array that keeps growing can become so expensive that the call runs out of gas and fails. Reading an index that does not exist, such as `scores[3]` in a list of three, also makes the call revert.

units.title: Mappings and structs
units.summary: Look up values by key with mappings, group values with structs and combine both into nested data.

lesson.md: A **mapping** stores one value for each key, like a dictionary. `mapping(string => uint256)` maps text keys to numbers. You read and write with square brackets: `ages[name]`. The calls here are `setAge("Ada", 36)`, `setAge("Alan", 41)`, `ages("Ada")` and `ages("Grace")`.
In a mapping, every key exists from the start and has the default value, so `ages("Grace")` returns 0. A mapping does not know its keys: you cannot loop over it or ask for its length.
The most common key is an `address`. With `msg.sender` as the key, every caller gets their own value. The calls are `earn(5)`, `earn(10)`, `points(you)` and `points(bob)`.

A **struct** groups related values into a new type. You create a value with the struct name and the fields in order, such as `Task("Learn Solidity", false)`, and read a field with a dot: `task.done`. The getter of a public struct returns all its fields. The calls are `task()`, `complete()` and `task()`.

lesson.output:
Learn Solidity, false
Learn Solidity, true

lesson.md: You can combine these types: an array of structs, a mapping to a struct or a mapping of mappings such as `mapping(address => mapping(uint256 => bool))`. `Task storage task = tasks[index];` gives a reference to the stored task, so a change to `task` changes the stored data. The calls are `add("Read")`, `add("Write")`, `complete(1)`, `tasks(0)` and `tasks(1)`.
`Task memory task = tasks[index];` makes a temporary copy. Changing the copy does not change the stored task. Use `storage` when you want to change stored data.

card: `storage` refers to stored data, `memory` is a copy

units.title: Events, errors and modifiers
units.summary: Tell the outside world what happened with events, fail with custom errors and reuse checks with modifiers.

lesson.md: A contract cannot print text. Instead it **emits events**: records in the log of the transaction that apps and websites can read. You declare an event with `event Name(type name);` and fire it with `emit Name(value);`. In the output, each emitted event adds a line that starts with `event`. Here you call `increase()` twice.

Events cost less gas than state variables, but a contract cannot read its own events later. With the word `indexed`, as in `event Paid(address indexed from, uint256 amount)`, apps can search for events with a certain value.

Instead of a text message you can define a **custom error**: `error Name(type name);`. You fail with `revert Name(value);`. Custom errors use less gas than messages and can carry values. The calls are `withdraw(60)`, `withdraw(60)` and `amount()`.

A **modifier** is a check that you can add to many functions. Its code runs before the function, and `_;` marks the place where the body of the function runs. The **constructor** runs only once, when the contract is deployed. It is often used to save the deployer as the owner.
Below, you deploy the contract and call `setPrice(20)`. Then Bob calls `setPrice(5)`, written as `bob: setPrice(5)`. Finally you call `price()`.
`require` with a message and `revert` with a custom error both stop the call and undo its changes. Many new contracts prefer custom errors because they are cheaper.
A modifier must contain `_;`. If the check comes after `_;`, the body of the function runs before the check.

units.title: A tiny token
units.summary: Build a small token with a balance for every address, a safe transfer function and checked arithmetic.

lesson.md: A **token** is a contract that keeps a balance for every address, like points or coins. Real tokens follow a standard called ERC-20. Here you build a tiny token with the core idea: a mapping of balances. The constructor takes a parameter, and you pass its value when you deploy. The examples deploy with `supply` set to `1000`. The calls are `balanceOf(you)` and `balanceOf(bob)`.

To move tokens, `transfer` checks that the caller has enough, subtracts the amount from the caller and adds it to the receiver. It uses `msg.sender`, so every caller can only move their own tokens. Nobody can fake `msg.sender`, because every transaction is signed with the key of its account. The calls are `transfer(bob, 300)`, `balanceOf(you)`, `balanceOf(bob)` and `bob: transfer(you, 500)`. Bob has only 300 tokens, so the last call reverts.

Since version 0.8, `+`, `-` and `*` are **checked**. If a result does not fit into its type, the call reverts with a `Panic` error and the code `0x11`. A `uint256` cannot go below 0, and a `uint8` holds only 0 to 255. Older versions silently wrapped around, for example from 255 to 0, and that caused real losses. The calls are `subtract(5, 3)`, `subtract(3, 5)` and `grow(255)`.

So even without a check, a transfer of too many tokens would revert. A check with a clear error is still better, because it tells the caller what went wrong. Code inside `unchecked { ... }` skips the checks and wraps around. Use it only when you are sure that no overflow can happen.

The final token has a name, a total supply, a `Transfer` event and a custom error. Deploy it with `1000`, then call `transfer(bob, 250)`, `bob: transfer(you, 300)`, `totalSupply()` and `balanceOf(bob)`.
Real ERC-20 tokens also have `approve`, `transferFrom` and `decimals`. Libraries such as OpenZeppelin offer tested versions that you can build on.
Code on a blockchain cannot be changed, and mistakes can lose real money. Test every contract well, and get it reviewed before it handles real value.
